tours.name: The Last Spike
tours.blurb: Gold Creek, September 8, 1883 — a golden spike, a borrowed president, and a territory changed in an afternoon.

keys.cap: Gold Creek, where the Northern Pacific's rails from both oceans met. Ulysses S. Grant drove the last spike — the same iron spike that had started the road in Minnesota in 1870.
Deer Lodge, division point in the valley — and later the heart of the Milwaukee's electrification, where boxcab motors swapped for steam.
Mullan Pass, where the NP bored the Continental Divide — 3,850 feet of tunnel under the pass Lieutenant Mullan's wagon road had crossed twenty years before.
Down Prickly Pear canyon to Helena — the gold capital finally on iron rails; freight rates fell by half within a year.

tours.name: Marias Pass
tours.blurb: The lowest crossing of the northern Rockies, hidden in plain sight until December 1889.

keys.cap: The Hi-Line. Jim Hill's Great Northern built west across the top of Montana in 1887 at a mile a day, aiming at a pass no railroad man had ever seen.

John F. Stevens walked into Marias Pass alone in December 1889, in forty below, and found the Blackfeet's long-known crossing: 5,213 feet, no tunnel needed — the lowest rail crossing of the Rockies between Canada and New Mexico.
Down the Middle Fork toward the Flathead — the line that would carry tourists to a park that didn't exist yet; the GN practically invented Glacier.
Whitefish, the division town the railway planted in the timber in 1904 — roundhouse first, town after.

tours.name: The Electrics
tours.blurb: In 1915 the Milwaukee Road strung 3,000-volt wire over the Belt and the Divide — the longest electrified railroad on earth.

keys.cap: Harlowton, where steam handed over to electricity — boxcab motors took every train west from here, 440 miles to Avery, Idaho.
Sixteenmile Canyon, threaded first by the rickety Montana Railroad — the 'Jawbone' — and rebuilt by the Milwaukee for its Pacific Extension.
Pipestone Pass, the Milwaukee's crossing of the Divide — electric motors regenerated current braking downgrade, feeding power back into the wire.
Butte, the richest customer on any line — four railroads fought for the hill's ore, and the copper they hauled came back as the trolley wire overhead.

tours.name: The Jawbone
tours.blurb: Richard Harlow built a railroad on promises through Sixteenmile Canyon — they said he financed it with his jaw.

keys.cap: Ringling, on the Jawbone — the Montana Railroad wandered from Lombard up Sixteenmile to White Sulphur country and on to Lewistown, broke the whole way.
Sixteenmile Canyon's goosenecks — track laid on shelves and trestles a wagon would refuse; the 1899 map in this gallery's wing was Harlow's own promotion.
Harlowton bears his name — and when the Milwaukee bought the Jawbone for its main line, Harlow's bluff became transcontinental track.
Lewistown and the Judith Basin — homestead country the Jawbone opened; the boxcars brought the settlers, then hauled their wheat, then hauled them away in the dry years.

tours.name: Four Ways West
tours.blurb: By 1912 four transcontinental routes crossed Montana — pull the slider back to 1884 and watch the web appear.

keys.cap: The whole state at once: Northern Pacific along the Yellowstone, Great Northern along the Hi-Line, the Milwaukee threading between them, the Burlington slipping in from the southeast.
Glendive, the NP's gateway division point on the Yellowstone — slide to 1884 and it is the only railroad in a territory of one line.
Havre, Hill's shop town on the Hi-Line — in 1884 this is empty shortgrass on the Fort Assinniboine military road.
Billings, the 'Magic City,' conjured by the NP on the Yellowstone in 1882 — by 1912 the Burlington and the GN reach it too, and the sugar-beet flats are drawn under wire.
